citation: Chaput JP, Despres JP, Bouchard C, Tremblay A. The association between sleep duration and weight gain in adults: a 6-year prospective study from the Quebec Family Study. Sleep. 2008;31(4):517-523.
your_quote: After adjustment for age, sex, and baseline BMI, short-duration sleepers gained 1.98 kg (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.16-2.82) more and long-duration sleepers gained 1.58 kg (95% CI: 1.02-2.56) more than did average-duration sleepers over 6 years.
your_note: Value taken directly on the target scale (kg gained over 6 years, short minus average sleepers). SE = (2.82 - 1.16)/3.92 = 1.66/3.92 = 0.4235. Exposure groups match the target: short-duration sleepers = 5-6 h (midpoint 5.5 h, matching target_exposure_dose_h) and average-duration sleepers = 7-8 h (midpoint 7.5 h, matching target_exposure_referent_h). n = 240 = short (21 men + 22 women = 43) + average (85 men + 112 women = 197); the adjusted model was fitted on the full longitudinal sample of 276 (117 men, 159 women), so an extractor could reasonably report 276 instead. Sign: positive = more weight gain under short sleep (worse outcome), which is the natural orientation for this raw-units target; the hedges_g/log_rr sign rules do not apply to a kg difference.

citation: Yang FN, Xie W, Wang Z. Effects of sleep duration on neurocognitive development in early adolescents in the USA: a propensity score matched, longitudinal, observational study. Lancet Child and Adolescent Health. 2022;6(10):705-712.
target_unit: Pearson r between baseline and 2-year effect-size maps for grey matter volume
your_quote: The pattern of Cohen's d on GMV in the 184 regions at baseline was significantly correlated with that at FL2 ( Figure 4C ; r = 0.52, 95% CI 0.40-0.61, p < 0.0001), suggesting that certain structural measures are consistently susceptible to insufficient sleep over time.
your_note: Exactly the targeted quantity: Pearson r between the baseline and 2-year (FL2) effect-size (Cohen's d) maps for grey matter volume. SE = (0.61 - 0.40)/3.92 = 0.21/3.92 = 0.0536. n = 184: the correlation is computed across 184 GMV regions, which are the units of this estimate. Verified arithmetically: Fisher z(0.52) = 0.576, and the reported CI corresponds to SE_z = 0.0728 = 1/sqrt(n-3), giving n ~ 192, consistent with 184 regions. The underlying participant sample was 3,021 matched sufficient-/insufficient-sleep pairs at baseline and 749 pairs at FL2; an extractor reporting participant N would give 749, so n is a likely disagreement point. Sign: this r measures persistence/stability of the group difference, not harm, so the hedges_g sign convention does not apply; target_exposure_dose_h and _referent_h are both 9.0 because the contrast is <9 h vs >=9 h of sleep. Design: propensity-score-matched longitudinal observational ABCD cohort with parent-reported sleep duration. The group contrasts at each wave are themselves cross-sectional, so cross_sectional/TX is a defensible alternative coding; propensity-score matching on observational data is not an exogenous assignment mechanism, so I did not code quasi_experiment.

citation: Schmid D, Erlacher D, Klostermann A, Kredel R, Hossner EJ. Sleep-dependent motor memory consolidation in healthy adults: A meta-analysis. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews. 2020;118:270-281.
your_quote: No positive effect of sleep in the deprivation design was found (g = -0.11, 95 % CI = [-0.66, 0.43]).
your_note: Deprivation-design subgroup of the design-level (task-independent) subgroup analysis, matching the target construct. SE = (0.43 - (-0.66))/3.92 = 1.09/3.92 = 0.2781. SIGN CAVEAT: the paper's effect measure is relative sleep gain (RSG = Hedges g of the sleep group minus Hedges g of the wake group), so it is oriented as a sleep BENEFIT. I report the paper's value verbatim (-0.11) because the target construct is explicitly named 'relative_sleep_gain'. Under the task's strict convention (negative = worse outcome under the deprived condition) the harmonised value would be +0.11, since RSG = -0.11 means the deprived group did marginally better. The estimate is near zero so the magnitude is unaffected. The identical value g = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.66, 0.43] is also reported in the finger-tapping-task-only subgroup analysis, because the deprivation-design studies all used the finger tapping task; this duplication is a possible source of confusion but not of disagreement. n = null: no participant count is given for the deprivation subgroup. Table 1's design column codes only ~2 sleep-wake group pairs as deprivation design (consistent with the very wide CI); the whole meta-analysis covered 48 studies, 53 sleep groups (n = 829) and 53 wake groups (n = 825). Tier ambiguity: the task's tier list assigns no tier to the meta-analysis design codes. I mapped tier by the underlying evidence base rather than defaulting to TX; an extractor treating meta-analysis as an unlisted design would code TX.

citation: Åkerstedt T, Ghilotti F, Grotta A, Zhao H, Adami HO, Trolle-Lagerros Y, Bellocco R. Sleep duration and mortality - Does weekend sleep matter? J Sleep Res. 2019 Feb;28(1):e12712.
your_quote: The weekday and weekend sleep duration analysis shows that for age <65 years group sleeping 5 hr or less, both during weekdays and weekend (SS), was associated with a 65% higher mortality rate (HR 1.65; 95% CI 1.22-2.23) compared with those consistently sleeping 6 or 7 hr per night (Figure 4 ).
your_note: Chosen because the referent matches the target exactly: the referent is 6-7 h per night (midpoint 6.5 h = target_exposure_referent_h) and the exposure is consistently <=5 h (= target_exposure_dose_h), i.e. the combined weekday/weekend sleep analysis in the <65 years stratum. log_hr = ln(1.65) = 0.5008. SE = (ln 2.23 - ln 1.22)/3.92 = (0.8020 - 0.1989)/3.92 = 0.1539. Positive = elevated mortality with short sleep, consistent with the task convention. Ambiguity: the paper's other short-sleep estimate is weekend-only sleep <=5 h vs a 7 h referent (HR 1.52; 95% CI 1.15-2.02); that referent is 7 h, not 6.5 h, so I did not use it. n = 38,015, the final analytic cohort after exclusions ('After applying the exclusion criteria, the final cohort consisted of 38,015 subjects'). The paper does not report the <65-year subgroup N separately, so the true n for this estimate is smaller and unstated.

citation: Jackson CL, Patel SR, Jackson WB 2nd, Lutsey PL, Redline S. Agreement between self-reported and objectively measured sleep duration among white, black, Hispanic, and Chinese adults in the United States: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis. Sleep. 2018;41(6):zsy057.
your_quote: Table 2. Unadjusted average differences/bias between self-reported and measured sleep duration (minutes) ... In-home PSG (for total sleep time)-one night (alloyed gold standard), Inter. (Bias) | Combined: 64 (59-69)
your_note: Taken from the 'Combined' (all races) row of Table 2, in-home PSG column: bias = 64 min (95% CI 59-69). Converted to the target scale (hours): 64/60 = 1.0667 h. SE in minutes = (69 - 59)/3.92 = 2.551 min; /60 = 0.0425 h. Positive = self-report longer than PSG, matching the target unit. Single-night PSG matches target_exposure_duration_days = 1. n = 1910 ('Among 1910 adults ...'). Ambiguity: the abstract reports only race-specific PSG biases (whites 73, blacks 54, Hispanics 67, Chinese 49 min), so an extractor working from the abstract alone would either pick one race or pool them; the Combined row in Table 2 is the correct overall value. Note also the actigraphy-based biases in the same row (TST 64 min, time in bed 49 min) - the actigraphy TST bias coincidentally also equals 64 min, but the target names PSG.

citation: Belenky G, Wesensten NJ, Thorne DR, Thomas ML, Sing HC, Redmond DP, Russo MB, Balkin TJ. Patterns of performance degradation and restoration during sleep restriction and subsequent recovery: a sleep dose-response study. Journal of Sleep Research. 2003;12(1):1-12.
your_quote: Table 4 Standard deviations of mean speed for each day and time in bed (TIB) group | 3-HR 5-HR 7-HR 9-HR | ... E7 1.0131 1.0149 0.7619 0.4723
your_note: No standardised effect size is reported; I computed Hedges' g for PVT mean speed on day E7 (7th restriction day, matching target_exposure_duration_days = 7), 3-h TIB vs 9-h TIB. SDs are taken verbatim from Table 4, row E7: SD(3-HR) = 1.0131, SD(9-HR) = 0.4723. Means were digitised from Figure 3 (no tabulated means exist): 3-HR = 2.349, 9-HR = 4.046 in units of (1/RT)*1000. Digitisation method: page rendered at high DPI; y-axis calibrated from the 10 detected tick rows (4.50 at row 328 to 2.25 at row 1374, 464.89 px per unit); marker centres located by dark-pixel profiling at the E7 tick column. Cross-check: the SDs implied by the digitised one-sided SEM error bars (0.9355 and 0.4344) agree with Table 4 to within ~8%, and the same calibration applied to Figure 2 reproduces the paper's stated 7.93 h mean TST for the 9-h group to within 1.7 min. Arithmetic: pooled SD = sqrt((12*1.0131^2 + 15*0.4723^2)/27) = 0.7616; d = (2.349 - 4.046)/0.7616 = -2.228; J = 1 - 3/(4*27-1) = 0.97196; g = -2.166. SE = sqrt(29/(13*16) + 2.166^2/(2*27)) = 0.476. Sign: negative = worse PVT speed under the 3-h restricted condition, per the task convention. n = 29 = 13 + 16, the final PVT analysis group sizes from Table 1 ('3 h (n = 13)', '9 h (n = 16)'); 66 volunteers were enrolled (3 h n = 18, 9 h n = 16) but PVT sessions were lost for some subjects, and the PVT ANOVA df (3, 52) confirms 56 analysable subjects. An extractor using the enrolment n of 34 would get g = -2.06 and SE = 0.43. Design: four parallel TIB groups in a residential laboratory study; the paper says subjects were 'assigned' to groups but never states random assignment, hence rob = some_concerns. lab_restriction_within_subject is an alternative code (the tier is T1 either way), though the specific contrast here is between-groups.

citation: Cohen S, Doyle WJ, Alper CM, Janicki-Deverts D, Turner RB. Sleep habits and susceptibility to the common cold. Arch Intern Med. 2009;169(1):62-67.
your_quote: The association with sleep efficiency was also graded with those with < 92% efficiency 5.50 times (CI[95%]=2.08-14.48) more likely to develop a cold than those with efficiencies >=98%.
your_note: Chose the sleep-EFFICIENCY contrast (<92% vs >=98%) rather than the sleep-duration contrast (<7 h vs >=8 h, OR 2.94, 95% CI 1.18-7.30) because target_exposure_type is 'other' with no dose or referent hours specified, which points to the non-duration exposure. This is a real ambiguity in the target specification and a plausible disagreement point. log_or = ln(5.50) = 1.7047. SE = (ln 14.48 - ln 2.08)/3.92 = (2.6728 - 0.7324)/3.92 = 0.4950. Positive = elevated risk with poorer sleep, consistent with the task convention. Outcome matches 'clinical cold ... objective criteria': the paper defines a clinical cold as 'infection in the presence of objective signs of illness'. target_exposure_duration_days = 14 matches the 14 consecutive days of sleep diaries. n = 153 ('Participants were 153 healthy men and women volunteers, ages 21-55'). Design: the viral challenge is experimental but the sleep exposure is observational and self-reported, measured prospectively over 14 days before the challenge, so prospective_cohort_selfreport / T5.

citation: Hinrichs P. When the Bell Tolls: The Effects of School Starting Times on Academic Achievement. Education Finance and Policy. 2011;6(4):486-507.
target_unit: SD of ACT score per hour later start
your_quote: For example, in the full specification of column 8, a 95 percent confidence interval for the effect of moving the school day back one hour is (-.2306, .1825). When expressed in terms of standard deviations of ACT scores, the confidence interval is (-.0512, .0406).
your_note: The paper reports no point estimate in SD units, only the SD-unit confidence interval, so I took its midpoint: (-0.0512 + 0.0406)/2 = -0.0053 SD of ACT per hour later start. SE = (0.0406 - (-0.0512))/3.92 = 0.0918/3.92 = 0.0234. Consistency check: the raw Table 3 column 8 coefficient is -0.3089/-0.0796/.../-0.0241 [SE 0.1036]; -0.0241 in raw ACT points maps to -0.0053 SD, implying an ACT SD of ~4.55, and 0.1036/4.55 = 0.0228, close to the CI-derived 0.0234 (I used the CI-derived value per the task's prescribed formula). n = 196,617 (reported for every column of Table 3). Sign: the exposure is one hour LATER school start (i.e. more sleep opportunity), so a negative value means marginally lower ACT scores with a later start; the effect is essentially zero and not significant. The hedges_g/log_rr sign rules do not apply to a per_hour_beta. Design: difference-in-differences exploiting Minneapolis's 2001 start-time change vs comparison districts, i.e. a quasi-experiment (T2).

citation: Twig G, Yaniv G, Levine H, Leiba A, Goldberger N, Derazne E, Ben-Ami Shor D, Tzur D, Afek A, Shamiss A, Haklai Z, Kark JD. Body-mass index in 2.3 million adolescents and cardiovascular death in adulthood. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(25):2430-2440.
your_quote: In calculations of the risk of death from total cardiovascular causes at different follow-up times and 10-year intervals, the association between cardiovascular mortality and increased BMI was evident by 10 years of follow-up (hazard ratio, 2.0; 95% CI, 1.1 to 3.9) and was more pronounced during the follow-up period from 30 to 40 years (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% CI, 3.1 to 5.4)
your_note: The 30-40-year follow-up stratum for death from total cardiovascular causes in the obese group (BMI >= 95th percentile) vs the 5th-24th percentile reference, matching the target construct. log_hr = ln(4.1) = 1.4110. SE = (ln 5.4 - ln 3.1)/3.92 = (1.6864 - 1.1314)/3.92 = 0.1416. Do not confuse with the overall (all follow-up) total-cardiovascular HR of 3.5 (95% CI 2.9-4.1), which shares the upper bound 4.1. n = 2,298,130 ('These exclusions resulted in a study sample of 2,298,130 participants'); the underlying stratum-specific n and death count for the 30-40-year window are in Table S5 of the supplementary appendix, which I did not retrieve. This is a comparator target (adolescent BMI, not a sleep exposure), so the sleep sign convention is not applicable; positive = elevated cardiovascular mortality with adolescent obesity. Design: prospective cohort with height and weight measured at a compulsory military medical examination, hence objective exposure (T4). rob = moderate: no adjustment for smoking, fitness, or adult BMI.

citation: Johns M, Hocking B. Daytime sleepiness and sleep habits of Australian workers. Sleep. 1997;20(10):844-849.
your_quote: ESS scores > 10 were taken to represent excessive daytime sleepiness, the prevalence of which was 10.9%.
your_note: Prevalence of excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale > 10) = 10.9% = 0.109 as a proportion. n = 330, derived from 'Sixty-five percent of all 507 employees working during the day for a branch of an Australian corporation answered a sleep questionnaire and the Epworth sleepiness scale (ESS) anonymously': 0.65 * 507 = 329.6. This is corroborated by the prevalence itself, since 36/330 = 10.909%, so 330 respondents with 36 cases is exactly consistent; the paper does not print the respondent count in the abstract. SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = sqrt(0.109 * 0.891/330) = 0.0172 (binomial, since no CI is given). Only the abstract was retrievable: the Oxford Academic PDF returns an HTML interstitial and no repository or PMC copy exists, so a full-text cross-check of the denominator was not possible; hence confidence medium. Design: single cross-sectional questionnaire survey of one employer's daytime workforce; rob = moderate given the 65% response rate and single-worksite sampling.

citation: Deng X, He M, He D, Zhu Y, Zhang Z, Niu W. Sleep duration and obesity in children and adolescents: evidence from an updated and dose-response meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine. 2021;78:169-181.
your_quote: In dose-response analyses, short sleep duration was significantly associated with obesity in toddlers (1-2 years) (adjusted RR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.07 to 1.34, P = 0.001), preschool-aged (3-5 years) children (1.58, 1.36 to 1.83, <0.001), and school-aged (6-13 years) children (1.82, 1.51 to 2.21, <0.001).
your_note: School-aged (6-13 y) stratum, matching the target construct: adjusted RR = 1.82 (95% CI 1.51-2.21). log_rr = ln(1.82) = 0.5988. SE = (ln 2.21 - ln 1.51)/3.92 = (0.7931 - 0.4121)/3.92 = 0.0972. Positive = elevated obesity risk with short sleep, consistent with the task convention. n = null: the meta-analysis pooled 33 articles with 57,848 children and adolescents overall, but no participant count is reported for the 6-13-year stratum. Design: pooled prospective cohorts with questionnaire-based sleep duration. The paper describes itself as a dose-response meta-analysis and labels these age strata as 'dose-response analyses', so dose_response_meta_analysis is a defensible alternative code; the estimate itself is a categorical short-vs-referent RR rather than a per-hour slope, which is why I coded meta_analysis_observational. Tier ambiguity: the task's tier list assigns no tier to the meta-analysis design codes. I mapped tier by the underlying evidence base rather than defaulting to TX; an extractor treating meta-analysis as an unlisted design would code TX.

citation: Belenky G, Wesensten NJ, Thorne DR, Thomas ML, Sing HC, Redmond DP, Russo MB, Balkin TJ. Patterns of performance degradation and restoration during sleep restriction and subsequent recovery: a sleep dose-response study. J Sleep Res. 2003;12(1):1-12.
your_quote: For all groups, TST amounts appeared to return to baseline values during recovery, i.e. B was not different from R1-R3 for any group.
your_note: The paper reports no numeric total sleep time for the 8-h TIB recovery nights in text or table, so I digitised Figure 2 ('Mean total daily sleep durations in minutes (and hours - right-hand ordinate) as a function of time in bed group'). Calibration: left axis ticks detected at 5 evenly spaced rows for 540/420/300/180/60 min (540 at row 126, 60 at row 1178; 0.45627 min/px); the 11 marker columns sit on the detected x-axis ticks. Validation: the digitised 9-h group mean over E1-E7 is 7.958 h against the paper's stated 7.93 h, an error of 1.7 min. Digitised recovery (R1/R2/R3) total sleep time at 8 h TIB: 9-HR 7.10/7.14/7.14 h; 7-HR 6.91/6.80/6.51 h; 5-HR 6.97/~6.88/6.64 h; the 3-HR open circles overlap the other markers and could not be isolated cleanly. Group-size-weighted grand mean ~= 7.0 h/night, which I report; digitised baseline (also 8 h TIB) is ~7.05 h, consistent with the quoted statement that recovery did not differ from baseline. se = null: the figure's error bars are described as standard errors but are not separable from the overlapping markers at R1-R3. n = 65, implied by the total sleep time ANOVA df (F3,61: 61 + 4 groups = 65). Confidence low because the value is figure-derived and the target construct is loosely specified: 'recuperative sleep ceiling at 8 h TIB' could mean total sleep time at 8 h TIB (my reading, ~7.0 h) or total sleep time net of stage 1, which the paper argues confers no recuperative benefit (that reading would give roughly 6.2-6.5 h). Note that 6.28 h, which looks like a candidate answer, is actually the 7-h TIB group's mean during the restriction phase, not a recovery value.

citation: Cappuccio FP, D'Elia L, Strazzullo P, Miller MA. Quantity and quality of sleep and incidence of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Diabetes Care. 2010 Feb;33(2):414-20.
target_unit: log RR, long sleep vs referent
your_quote: For short duration of sleep (<=5-6 h/night), the RR was 1.28 (95% CI 1.03-1.60, P = 0.024, heterogeneity P = 0.015); for long duration of sleep (>8-9 h/night), the RR was 1.48 (1.13-1.96, P = 0.005)
your_note: Long-sleep pooled estimate: RR = 1.48 (95% CI 1.13-1.96). log_rr = ln(1.48) = 0.3920. SE = (ln 1.96 - ln 1.13)/3.92 = (0.6729 - 0.1222)/3.92 = 0.1405. TARGET SPECIFICATION PROBLEM: target_exposure_type is 'habitual_short_sleep', but target_outcome_construct ('incident_type_2_diabetes_long_sleep') and target_unit ('log RR, long sleep vs referent') both specify LONG sleep. I extracted the long-sleep estimate as the construct and unit direct. Consequently the task's sign rule ('POSITIVE means elevated risk with short sleep') is inapplicable: positive here means elevated diabetes risk with LONG sleep. If a first extractor followed target_exposure_type instead, they would have taken the short-sleep RR of 1.28 (log_rr 0.2469, SE 0.1124), which would be a large disagreement traceable to the target, not the source. Dose ambiguity: the pooled long-sleep category is '>8-9 h/night' (primary studies defined it as >8 or >=9 h). A sensitivity analysis restricted to studies defining long sleep as >9 h gives RR 1.38 (95% CI 1.15-1.65, n = 5 cohorts), which matches target_exposure_dose_h = 9 more literally; I used the primary 1.48 because it is the headline estimate for the named construct. n = null: the long-sleep analysis drew on 7 population cohorts from 6 published prospective studies and no participant count is given for it; the whole review covered 107,756 participants across 10 studies / 13 cohorts with 3,586 incident cases. Design: pooled prospective cohorts, all assessing sleep by questionnaire (one by interview). Tier ambiguity: the task's tier list assigns no tier to the meta-analysis design codes. I mapped tier by the underlying evidence base rather than defaulting to TX; an extractor treating meta-analysis as an unlisted design would code TX.

citation: Chinoy ED, Cuellar JA, Huwa KE, Jameson JT, Watson CH, Bessman SC, Hirsch DA, Cooper AD, Drummond SPA, Markwald RR. Performance of seven consumer sleep-tracking devices compared with polysomnography. Sleep. 2021;44(5):zsaa291.
target_unit: minutes (positive = device OVERestimates sleep vs PSG)
your_note: Table 1 (total sleep time vs PSG), Fitbit Alta HR row: n = 49 device-nights, PSG mean 425.1 +/- 33.1 min, device mean 427.7 +/- 19.7 min, bias = +2.6 min, limits of agreement -42.0 to 47.1, t = 0.8 (p = 0.421). Positive = the device OVERestimates sleep relative to PSG, matching the target unit; the bias is not statistically significant. SE derivation: the limits of agreement are +/- 2 SD from the bias, so SD of the paired differences = (47.1 - (-42.0))/4 = 22.275 min, and SE = 22.275/sqrt(49) = 3.18 min. Cross-check against the reported t: 2.6/3.18 = 0.82, matching the tabulated t = 0.8; inverting the one-significant-figure t instead gives 2.6/0.8 = 3.25, so 3.18 is the more precise value. n = 49 device-nights contributed by 20 participants who used the Fitbit Alta HR; target_exposure_duration_days = 3 matches the three consecutive test nights. Reporting device-nights rather than participants (20) is a possible disagreement point. Design: device-validation study against PSG with no exposure contrast, hence normative_descriptive / TX; rob low (in-laboratory PSG reference, time-synced devices, pre-specified summary metrics).

citation: Berres S, Erdfelder E. The sleep benefit in episodic memory: An integrative review and a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. 2021;147(12):1309-1353.
your_quote: We observed a moderate sleep benefit in episodic memory for the complete data set, g = 0.44, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.39, 0.50], t(252.26) = 16.94, p < .001, k = 823, m = 271.
your_note: Overall (intercept-only three-level model with robust variance estimation) sleep benefit in episodic memory. The SE is reported directly as 0.03; the CI-derived value agrees: (0.50 - 0.39)/3.92 = 0.028. SIGN CAVEAT: the paper's metric is oriented as a sleep benefit, so +0.44 means better recall after sleep than after wake. Under the task's strict convention (negative = worse outcome under the shorter-sleep/restricted condition) the harmonised value would be -0.44, since the wake condition is the sleep-deprived arm. I report the paper's +0.44 because the target construct is explicitly named 'episodic_memory_sleep_benefit_overall' and target_exposure_type is 'descriptive'; sign is a likely disagreement point. n = null: no participant total is reported for the overall estimate, which pools k = 823 effect sizes from m = 271 independent samples in 177 articles. rob = some_concerns: the authors flag selective reporting as a threat, and the effect falls to g = 0.28 after correcting for funnel-plot asymmetry (median 0.41 across 20 three-parameter selection-model subsets). Retrieval: the published abstract and the author's dissertation give g = 0.44 without an SE; the SE came from the full accepted manuscript. Tier ambiguity: the task's tier list assigns no tier to the meta-analysis design codes. I mapped tier by the underlying evidence base rather than defaulting to TX; an extractor treating meta-analysis as an unlisted design would code TX.

citation: Wang J, Li AM, Lam HSHS, Leung GM, Schooling CM. Sleep Duration and Adiposity in Children and Adults: Observational and Mendelian Randomization Studies. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2019;27(6):1013-1022.
your_quote: Longer sleep was cross-sectionally associated with lower BMI z score at ~11 years of age (-0.13 per category, 95% CI: -0.22 to -0.04)
your_note: Observational cross-sectional arm at ~11 years in the Hong Kong 'Children of 1997' birth cohort, matching the target construct. SE = (-0.04 - (-0.22))/3.92 = 0.18/3.92 = 0.0459. SIGN: the paper reports the association per category of LONGER sleep, so -0.13 means longer sleep goes with lower BMI z. Oriented per category of SHORTER sleep (target_exposure_type = habitual_short_sleep) the value would be +0.13, i.e. higher BMI z with less sleep. This orientation flip is the most likely disagreement point here. n = null: the abstract does not state the analytic sample size for the age-11 cross-sectional analysis. The article is closed access with no repository or PMC copy (OpenAlex reports oa_status 'closed'; publisher access is blocked by bot protection), so I could not retrieve it. The sample sizes in the abstract (35,668 children; 152,893 men; 171,977 women) belong to the separate Mendelian randomisation arm and must not be used here. Design: this target names the cross-sectional observational estimate, so design is cross_sectional / TX even though the study's headline contribution is Mendelian randomisation (which would be mendelian_randomization / T3 for a different target).

citation: Bixler EO, Fernandez-Mendoza J, Liao D, Calhoun S, Rodriguez-Colon SM, Gaines J, He F, Vgontzas AN. Natural history of sleep disordered breathing in prepubertal children transitioning to adolescence. Eur Respir J. 2016;47(5):1402-1409.
your_quote: The incidence of adolescent AHI >=2 events per h in those with childhood AHI <2 events per h was 36.5%, while the incidence of AHI >=5 events per h in those with childhood AHI <5 events per h was 10.6%.
your_note: Incidence of adolescent apnoea-hypopnoea index >= 5 events/h among those without childhood AHI >= 5, matching the target construct: 10.6% = 0.106 as a proportion. Table 2 gives the underlying counts, 44/415 (10.6), confirming n = 415 with 44 incident cases. SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = sqrt(0.106 * 0.894/415) = 0.0151 (binomial, since no CI is reported). This is a descriptive baseline-risk quantity, not an exposure-outcome contrast, so no sign convention applies. Design: population-based prospective cohort with in-laboratory polysomnography at both waves (mean 8.4 years apart), hence objective measurement (T4); normative_descriptive is a defensible alternative given target_exposure_type = 'descriptive'. rob = moderate: 421 of 700 invited subjects returned (60% response), though the authors report no baseline demographic differences between participants and non-participants.

citation: Lo JC, Bennion KA, Chee MWL. Sleep restriction can attenuate prioritization benefits on declarative memory consolidation. Journal of Sleep Research. 2016;25(6):664-672.
your_quote: There was no main effect of group ( F (1,43) = 1.13, P = 0.29, etap 2 = 0.026), nor was there an interaction between group and prioritization
your_note: The paper reports no Cohen's d for the overall (total) free-recall group difference, so I converted the group main effect F from the repeated-measures ANOVA: d = 2*sqrt(F/df_denom) = 2*sqrt(1.13/43) = 0.324. Cross-check via partial eta squared: 2*sqrt(0.026/(1-0.026)) = 0.327. SIGN: negative because the sleep-restricted group recalled less at every time point in Figure 2 (1 week: sleep restriction 81.8% highlighted / 67.4% non-highlighted vs control 87.2% / 71.1%), i.e. worse performance under the 5-h condition, per the task convention. The difference is not statistically significant. SE = sqrt((n1+n2)/(n1*n2) + d^2/(2*(n1+n2-2))) = sqrt(45/(22.5*22.5) + 0.324^2/86) = 0.30, assuming an even split of the 45 analysed participants (the per-group split at 6 weeks is not reported). n = 45, implied by the quoted F's denominator df (43 + 2). 56 adolescents were randomised (and the initial and 1-week paired tests use t(55), i.e. 56); attrition left 45 with complete 6-week data. An extractor reporting 56 would get SE = 0.27. Ambiguity: the group main effect pools all three retrieval delays (initial, 1 week, 6 weeks); no separate total-recall group test is reported for the 1-week timepoint alone, which is what target_exposure_duration_days = 7 most directly implies. Design: randomised parallel-group 5-h vs 9-h sleep-opportunity trial (indexed as a Randomized Controlled Trial), polysomnography-verified; rob low.

citation: Åkerstedt T, Ghilotti F, Grotta A, Bellavia A, Lagerros YT, Bellocco R. Sleep duration, mortality and the influence of age. Eur J Epidemiol. 2017 Oct;32(10):881-891.

your_quote: Table 4 shows that at the 25th percentile of age at death, short and long sleepers died 8.5 (95% CI -16.7; -0.4) and 6.6 months (95% CI -12.4; -0.7) earlier, respectively.

citation: Basner M, Hermosillo E, Nasrini J, Saxena S, Dinges DF, Moore TM, Gur RC. Cognition test battery: Adjusting for practice and stimulus set effects for varying administration intervals in high performing individuals. J Clin Exp Neuropsychol. 2020;42(5):516-529.

your_note: Table 3, PVT row of the speed domain: raw estimate per log_e(administration number) = 0.0126 (SE 0.0163) and standardized estimate = 0.02 (SE 0.03), p = 0.44. SIGN CAVEAT: the PVT's speed-domain outcome in this table is SLOWNESS (10 - 1/s), not speed, so +0.02 SD means marginally SLOWER with repeated administration. citation: Dewald JF, Meijer AM, Oort FJ, Kerkhof GA, Bogels SM. The influence of sleep quality, sleep duration and sleepiness on school performance in children and adolescents: A meta-analytic review. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2010;14(3):179-189.
your_quote: The meta-analysis yielded a small overall effect size (z = 0.135; p < 0.001 (CI [ 0.149; 0.121]), r = 0.134, fixed model; z = 0.134; p < 0.001 (CI [ 0.182; 0.085]), r = 0.133, random model), indicating that lower sleepiness scores are associated with better school performance.
your_note: Overall random-effects correlation between sleepiness and school performance: r = -0.133. SIGN: the minus signs are lost by the PDF text extraction (the quote shows bare '0.133', '0.182', '0.085'), but the direction is fixed by the same sentence, 'lower sleepiness scores are associated with better school performance', so the correlation is negative: more sleepiness goes with worse school performance. The abstract likewise prints the magnitude without a sign ('Sleepiness showed the strongest relation to school performance (r = 0.133)'), so an extractor could plausibly report +0.133 - a likely sign disagreement. SE: the CI is on the Fisher z scale, so SE_z = (0.182 - 0.085)/3.92 = 0.024745; converted to the r scale via SE_r = SE_z * (1 - r^2) = 0.024745 * 0.98232 = 0.0243. I used the random-effects estimate (r = -0.133) rather than the fixed-effects one (r = -0.134, much narrower CI [-0.149, -0.121], SE_z 0.00714) because heterogeneity was significant (Q(16) = 155.7, p < 0.001); the choice barely changes the point estimate but changes the SE by more than threefold, so it is the main disagreement risk here. n = 19,530 across 17 studies ('17 studies sleepiness (N = 19,530)'). Design/tier: pooled observational studies, of which 'The majority of the studies was cross-sectional in design' (one longitudinal study contributed its first wave only), so the pooled evidence base is cross-sectional and I coded TX. citation: Killick R, Hoyos CM, Melehan KL, Dungan GC 2nd, Poh J, Liu PY. Metabolic and hormonal effects of 'catch-up' sleep in men with chronic, repetitive, lifestyle-driven sleep restriction. Clin Endocrinol (Oxf). 2015 Oct;83(4):498-507.
target_unit: 10^-4 /min/(uU/ml) difference in minimal-model insulin sensitivity (10 h minus 6 h)
your_quote: Insulin sensitivity (ISx) was significantly increased following three nights of 'catch-up' sleep (10 h) compared to continuing sleep restriction (6 h) (8.57 x 10 -4 /min/(uU/ml), (1.1, 16.1 x 10 -4 ; P = 0.03) (Fig. 3 a).
your_note: The reported quantity matches the target unit exactly: the 10 h minus 6 h difference in minimal-model insulin sensitivity, 8.57 x 10^-4 /min/(uU/ml), 95% CI 1.1 to 16.1 x 10^-4, after 3 nights (target_exposure_duration_days = 3). SE = (16.1 - 1.1)/3.92 = 15.0/3.92 = 3.83. Sign: positive = better insulin sensitivity with 10 h catch-up sleep than with continued 6 h restriction, i.e. recovery sleep helps. n = 8, the number completing the relevant condition pairing ('10 h TIB/6 h TIB: n = 8'). 19 men completed the study overall, but each did only two of three possible conditions, so 19 would overstate the n for this contrast - a likely disagreement point. Design: in-laboratory randomised two-period crossover with computer-generated randomisation lists and >=3 weeks washout. rob = some_concerns: very small n, no blinding of the sleep condition, and an incomplete (partially confounded) design in which older men could not be allocated to the slow-wave-sleep-suppression arm.
